## Stress has a chemistry too

Brain receptors ([2.1](01-brain-action.qmd)) and brain rhythms ([2.2](02-brainwaves.qmd)) are two windows on tea's dual story. This sitting opens a third: **stress hormones**—what happens when the day itself is noisy.

When you are stressed, the body runs a loop often called the **HPA axis** (brain → pituitary → adrenals). One output is **cortisol**, a main stress hormone. Another related signal is **epinephrine** (adrenaline).

::: {.callout-tip title="Words to know in this sitting"}
- **HPA axis** — stress-hormone loop from brain to adrenals.
- **Cortisol** — a main stress hormone.
- **Epinephrine (adrenaline)** — a fast sympathetic "go" signal.
- **Salivary alpha-amylase (sAA)** — a stress-linked enzyme often used as a sympathetic marker.
- **Tolerance / adaptation** — repeated caffeine can blunt *caffeine-driven* cortisol spikes; stress can still ring the alarm.
:::

## Plain takeaways (then the fine print)

Plain takeaways from the packs and the papers behind them:

- Caffeine can activate the HPA axis and raise cortisol.
- L-theanine co-use is studied for keeping stress markers nearer baseline under cognitive or real-life load.
- Unmitigated caffeine can raise epinephrine, with blood-pressure and vessel-tone effects; L-theanine is described as helping keep pressure steadier via nitric-oxide–related relaxation in cell work—and has human data on blood pressure under stress.[^1][^2][^3]

Imagine a fire alarm (stress) and also a loud caffeine "boost" siren. Habitual caffeine use can quiet the *caffeine* siren over days. The fire alarm of real stress can still ring—and L-theanine is studied for blunting *stress*-linked responses even after caffeine habit forms.

| Measure | Condition | Finding | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Heart rate / salivary IgA under arithmetic stress | L-theanine vs placebo | L-theanine reduced heart-rate and salivary immune-stress responses; HRV pattern suggested less sympathetic drive | Kimura et al. (2007)[^1] |
| Blood pressure / tension-anxiety under mental tasks | L-theanine vs placebo | L-theanine attenuated BP rise in high-response adults and lowered Tension-Anxiety scores vs placebo | Yoto et al. (2012)[^3] |
| Morning salivary alpha-amylase during stressful practice | ~200 mg L-theanine twice daily vs placebo | Theanine group showed lower pre-practice sAA and lower subjective stress during a multi-day pharmacy practice | Unno et al. (2013)[^4] |
| Salivary cortisol across the day | 250 mg caffeine challenges after controlled intake weeks | After abstinence, caffeine raised cortisol robustly; after ~5 days at 300–600 mg/day, morning challenge responses were blunted but not all-day abolished | Lovallo et al. (2005)[^5] |

::: {.callout-important collapse="true" title="Honesty note: where pack tables and papers diverge"}
Some companion pack tables attribute a neat salivary-cortisol delta (L-theanine ~±5% vs placebo ~+22%) to **Yoto et al. (2012)**. The published Yoto 2012 paper measures **blood pressure and mood under stress**, not that cortisol contrast.[^3] This lesson therefore cites Yoto for BP/anxiety, Kimura for HR/sIgA, Unno for sAA under real student stress, and Lovallo for caffeine–cortisol adaptation—and does **not** repeat the mismatched cortisol attribution as fact.

Pack tables also sometimes phrase caffeine–cortisol adaptation as "nearly gone within five days." Lovallo's controlled trial is more precise: after five days at 300 or 600 mg/day, the **morning** caffeine-challenge cortisol response was largely abolished, but cortisol could still rise later in the day after further doses—**reduced, not eliminated**.[^5]
:::

## Myth check: "Caffeine permanently wrecks your adrenals"

Acute caffeine can raise cortisol a lot. With daily use in the hundreds of milligrams, that caffeine-driven spike often shrinks within about five days of controlled intake—but Lovallo's data say **incomplete** tolerance at everyday levels, not permanent adrenal destruction and not a total mute button.[^5] Stress-driven responses can still rise, which is exactly where L-theanine studies (Kimura, Yoto, Unno) earn their keep.[^1][^3][^4] Systematic reviews of L-theanine and stress/anxiety stay cautious: effects exist in some trials, but dose, setting, and outcome measure matter.[^6]

## Vessel tone is part of the same chapter

Caffeine can constrict cerebral vessels as part of its adenosine blockade story.[^7] L-theanine has been shown in cell work to promote nitric-oxide production in endothelial cells—one plausible path for "steadier pressure" language in the packs.[^2] Yoto's human stress design adds a behavioral-physiology bridge: L-theanine can blunt task-related blood-pressure climbs in high-responders.[^3] That is mechanism-plus-trial talk, not a home blood-pressure prescription.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: cortisol, amylase, and the five-day caffeine adaptation"}
| Measure | Condition | Finding | Trail |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Heart rate / salivary IgA under arithmetic stress | L-theanine vs placebo | Lower HR and stress-linked immune marker; HRV pattern → less sympathetic drive | Kimura et al. (2007)[^1] |
| BP / Tension-Anxiety under mental tasks | L-theanine vs placebo | Attenuated BP rise in high-responders; lower Tension-Anxiety | Yoto et al. (2012)[^3] |
| Morning sAA during pharmacy practice | **200 mg** L-theanine ×2/day vs placebo | Lower pre-practice sAA and lower subjective stress in theanine group | Unno et al. (2013)[^4] |
| Salivary cortisol to caffeine challenges | **250 mg** caffeine after 0 / 300 / 600 mg/day weeks | Abstinence → robust rise; 5 days intake → morning response blunted, later-day rises still possible | Lovallo et al. (2005)[^5] |

**Adaptation nuance.** Acute caffeine can raise cortisol a lot. Habitual intake reduces that caffeine-driven spike within days, but Lovallo concludes responses are **reduced, not eliminated** at intake levels common in daily life.[^5] Stress-driven markers can still move—and L-theanine is studied for blunting those *stress*-linked responses.[^1][^3][^4][^6]

Cell work showing L-theanine promoting endothelial nitric-oxide production is a plausible "steadier pressure" mechanism—not a home blood-pressure prescription.[^2]
:::

## A bridge into Chapter 4

This hormone thread also reaches forward into Chapter 4: when stress hormones rise, people can become more aggressive risk seekers in some lab settings. Softened loss aversion under pressure is one of the bridges on the [Linkages](../../linkages.qmd) page.

Hormones are still somewhat invisible. What can you see on the outside of the body?


## Story in one minute

Stress runs the HPA loop toward cortisol and related signals. Caffeine can push that loop; habitual intake blunts caffeine-driven cortisol spikes incompletely. L-theanine is studied for keeping heart rate, blood pressure, salivary stress enzymes, and subjective stress nearer baseline under load. Pack tables that mis-attribute cortisol numbers to Yoto 2012 are corrected here: Yoto is BP/mood; Lovallo is caffeine–cortisol adaptation.

## What this means when you drink tea

- "I adapted to coffee" ≠ "stress no longer raises cortisol."[^5]
- L-theanine stress findings are often **task** or **real-life stress** designs (Kimura arithmetic; Unno pharmacy practice)—not magic on a sofa.[^1][^4]
- Vessel/BP talk is supportive physiology, not a treatment plan.[^2][^3]

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: which paper answers which question?"}
| Question | Better primary trail |
| --- | --- |
| Does L-theanine reduce HR / stress markers under acute lab stress? | Kimura et al. (2007)[^1] |
| Does L-theanine blunt BP / tension under mental tasks? | Yoto et al. (2012)[^3] |
| Does multi-day theanine change sAA / subjective stress in real student stress? | Unno et al. (2013)[^4] |
| Does daily caffeine blunt caffeine-driven cortisol? | Lovallo et al. (2005) — reduced, not eliminated[^5] |
| Do reviews stay cautious? | Williams et al. (2020)[^6] |

Keeping the question matched to the paper is how this course stays honest when secondary tables blur together.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Click for more detail: take-home checklist for Lesson 2.3"}
1. HPA → cortisol; caffeine can push it.
2. Habituation ≠ zero stress chemistry.[^5]
3. L-theanine evidence is marker- and setting-specific.[^1][^3][^4]
4. Correct pack/paper mismatches when you see them.
5. Next: body meters you can measure without a hormone assay.
:::
